title: Are people drinking less alcohol?
intro: When was the last time you had an alcoholic drink? Some people choose to live without drinking any alcohol, but for many others drinking alcohol is a normal part of life. Even so, in recent generations many people have chosen to stop drinking alcohol. Georgie and Neil discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.
this_week_question: Many people in the UK and other countries choose to give up alcohol in the new year for the whole of the month of January, but what is the challenge called?
a) No-drink New Year b) Alcohol-free January c) Dry January
Listen to the programme to hear the answer.

vocab.desc: not drinking alcohol or taking recreational drugs societal pressure feeling that you should do something because lots of other people expect you to the norm the usual or common thing to do self-optimisation content videos, posts and other media about being fit, healthy and achieving big goals tout praise something or talk about it a lot to get others to try it pushback strong criticism of a trend; people doing the opposite of a trend

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Hi Neil.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Hi Georgie. Do you want to hear something quite unusual for me?

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Err, yes!

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: I haven't had an alcoholic drink this year.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Wow! That is really impressive. How do you feel? Like a new person?

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: I do feel very good, I have to say.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: I can't say the same – I did have a few alcoholic drinks at the weekend with my friends. But in many parts of the world, people don't drink alcohol at all. In the UK it's very common – that is until recently. Today on 6 Minute English, we're going to find out why many people are choosing to give up or cut down on alcohol, and we'll be asking, "Is this the end of British drinking culture?"

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: OK. Neil, let's start with a quiz question. Many people in the UK and other countries choose to give up alcohol in the new year for the whole of the month of January, but what is the challenge called? Is it: a)    No-drink New Year b)    Alcohol-free January, or c)    Dry January?

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Well, I know the answer to this, but I'm not going to give it away.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: OK. Well, then our listeners can find out the answer at the end of the programme.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Yes, they can. So, Georgie, I hear all the time that younger people don't drink as much alcohol today as they used to in the past. Is that true?

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, in the UK, surveys suggest that 16 to 24-year-olds are more likely to be non-drinkers than the older generations.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: OK. So, why are more young people choosing to be sober ? That means not to drink alcohol.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, the BBC World Service podcast What in the World have been investigating this. Presenter Hannah Gelbart met three young people who choose to be sober for some alcohol-free drinks to find out more. Here's Daniel's story:

transcript.author: Daniel
transcript.text: Yeah. So, today I don't drink at all, but when I was in my early 20s, I think I felt maybe a bit of, like, societal pressure – you know, work drinks or being at uni, where it was the norm to just join in. I think you'd probably get a few weird glances if you're like, "Yeah, I'm not going to join in at all." So, I did that and I think Covid lockdown just gave me a bit of confidence to say, "OK, let me step away from this. It's not necessarily something I want to do moving forward."

transcript.author: Hannah Gelbart
transcript.text: So, how many years have you been sober for?

transcript.author: Daniel
transcript.text: I would say it's been six years now.

transcript.author: Hannah Gelbart
transcript.text: Six years?

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: So, Daniel says that when he was younger, he felt societal pressure to drink alcohol. Societal pressure is feeling like you need to do something because lots of people around you are doing it.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Right. So, Daniel says drinking was the norm at university and after work. The norm is a way of saying that something is normal or common.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: But during the Covid-19 pandemic, when people in the UK were unable to socialise and visit pubs and bars, Daniel's attitude to alcohol changed. After that, he decided to be sober and he hasn't had a drink for about six years.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: So, Georgie, it seems like many young people don't drink at all and lots of them share their experience of being sober on social media. But recently there's been a bit of a change, hasn't there?

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes. Whilst many people use social media to share their experience of drinking less alcohol or no alcohol at all, some people have been saying that they want to go out more and drink and have fun with friends. They argue we're too worried about fitness and wellness, and that drinking some alcohol to have a good time is fine. Here's Millie talking more about this to BBC World Service podcast What in the World:

transcript.author: Millie
transcript.text: I think we had this, like, rise of self-optimisation content . I think unfortunately sobriety, kind of, got swept in with that and it got touted as this way to, you know, get up at 5am, do a HYROX. And, you know, for many of us, that's probably not our reality with not drinking. It's that we do it to feel a bit more sane or, you know, things like that. And so, I think now we are entering this, like, almost pushback era of that content and you're seeing celebrities... Like, it's not just alcohol – you're seeing more celebrities smoking and, like, posting that on their Instagram and not worrying if it's brand-friendly.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: OK. So, Millie thinks that being sober is associated with certain kinds of self-optimisation content , where people talk about fitness, diet and having big goals for themselves.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes, and Millie says being sober gets touted as a way to get up at 5am to exercise. In other words, people talk about it a lot and try to encourage people to do it.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: But Millie says that being sober isn't always about being super fit and healthy. For her, it's about being sane.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: But still, Millie thinks there's a pushback against self-optimisation content . Pushback means a criticism of the content, and people are pushing back by doing the opposite. For example, lots of celebrities post about themselves drinking and smoking.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Well, Georgie, I've decided to try to give up alcohol for a whole year, but I don't think everybody should do that if they don't want to. It's really up to the individual.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Yeah, I still enjoy having a few drinks with my friends. I think it's just all about balance, really. OK. Neil, it's time to reveal the answer to this week's question. I asked, "What was the name given for when people give up alcohol in January?"

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Yes. And the answer is Dry January.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: That is correct. Well done! Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with sober , which describes someone who doesn't drink alcohol or take recreational drugs.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Societal pressure is the feeling that you should do something because lots of other people expect you to.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Saying something is the norm is a way to say it's usual or common.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Self-optimisation content means videos and posts about being fit, healthy and achieving big goals.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: If somebody touts an idea or lifestyle, they talk about it a lot and try to convince people to do it.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: And pushback is strong criticism of a trend, and people doing the opposite.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but don't forget to test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Thank you for joining us and goodbye.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Goodbye!
